claims.text: The size of a market is the total sales in it over a stated period. It is measured either by volume, which is the number of units sold, or by value, which is what those units sold for.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Market size by value = units sold in the market x the average price paid. Market growth over a period = (size at the end - size at the start) / size at the start, expressed as a percentage. Market share = one business's sales / total market sales, expressed as a percentage, calculated either on value or on volume, with the basis stated because the two give different answers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because value carries price inside it and volume does not, the two measures of market size can move in opposite directions: a market in which fewer units are sold at higher prices grows in value while it shrinks in volume. A business planning capacity needs the volume figure and a business planning revenue needs the value figure, so quoting one where the decision turns on the other misstates the market.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Market growth measures how fast the market itself is changing, which separates sales a business won because the market expanded from sales it took from rivals. How the share is divided between competitors indicates how much of the market is realistically open: where a few established producers hold most of the share, a new entrant is likely to have to win customers away from one of them rather than find uncommitted buyers, and that usually requires a lower price or a clear point of difference.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The customer is the person or organisation that buys the product. The consumer is the person who uses it. They are frequently the same person; where they are not, the buying decision and the experience of the product sit with different people, so research has to reach both.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A customer profile is a description of the typical buyer of a product, built from characteristics such as age, income, occupation, gender, location, household situation, lifestyle and buying behaviour - how often they buy, how much they spend and what prompts the purchase.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A need is something the consumer must have for basic living or for the product to do its job at all. A want is a preference for one particular way of meeting that need. Competing products in a market usually meet the same need, so the choice between them is normally settled by wants.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A profile made of characteristics the business can act on - where these buyers are, what they can afford, when and how often they buy - lets the business match the product, the price, the place of sale and the promotion to those buyers, so spending is directed at people whose stated characteristics make them likely buyers instead of being spread across a whole population. A profile built from characteristics the business cannot act on changes nothing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Primary research, also called field research, is the collection of new data first-hand, by the business or by a firm it commissions, for the particular question the business is trying to answer. Its usual methods are questionnaires and surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation and test marketing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Secondary research, also called desk research, is the use of data that already exists because it was collected for some other purpose. Internal secondary sources are the business's own records - sales figures, customer records, past reports. External secondary sources include government and central-bank statistics, trade association figures, published market reports, competitors' public material, news reporting and data published online.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: What separates primary from secondary data is who collected it and for what purpose, not whether it is numbers or words and not how it was gathered. Data the business collected itself for the question in hand is primary however informal the method; data someone else collected for another purpose is secondary however closely it fits the question.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Primary data is collected to the business's own specification - its sample, its questions, its timing - and is held by the business unless it releases it. Secondary data already exists, so it can usually be obtained in days rather than weeks and at a much lower cost, but its age, its coverage, its definitions and the method behind it were all fixed by whoever collected it and cannot be changed afterwards.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Primary data is useful mainly because it answers the question the business actually asked: the people sampled, the wording of the questions, the timing and the level of detail are all chosen by the business, so the findings arrive in a form the decision can use without adjustment.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because primary data is commissioned by the business and held by it, rivals are unlikely to hold the same findings, so a move based on it may take longer for a competitor to anticipate or match than one based on a report anyone can buy.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The usefulness of primary data is limited by cost and by time - fieldwork has to be designed, carried out and analysed before any answer exists - and by the quality of the fieldwork itself. A sample that does not represent the target market, questions that suggest their own answer, and respondents who say what sounds reasonable rather than what they will actually do all produce data that is precise about the wrong thing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Primary research repays its cost where the decision is large enough that being wrong is expensive, where no existing data answers the question, and where there is time to collect and analyse it before the decision has to be made. Where any of those conditions fails, secondary sources or a smaller and narrower primary study are likely to be the better use of the same money.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Secondary data is useful because it exists already: it can be obtained quickly and at low cost, it often covers a whole market or a long run of years that no single business could afford to survey, and it establishes market size, growth and structure before the business spends anything on fieldwork.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Secondary data was collected for someone else's purpose, so its definitions, categories, geographic coverage and dates may not match the question being asked. It may be out of date. The method behind it is sometimes not published, so its reliability cannot be judged from the figures alone. And where it is publicly available, competitors can read the same figures, so it rarely produces an advantage none of them has.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal secondary data - the business's own sales records, customer records and past reports - is cheap, already in the business's own categories and usually current, but it describes the people who already buy from the business, so it says little about the part of the market the business has not reached and nothing about why people who did not buy stayed away.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Secondary research is usually the sensible first step rather than the whole answer: it establishes cheaply what is already known, which narrows the primary research to the questions only fieldwork can settle and so reduces the cost of the fieldwork that follows.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The target population is everyone the findings are meant to describe. A sample is the part of that population actually researched, and sampling is the process of selecting it. A result taken from the sample is used as an estimate of the result that would have been obtained from the whole population.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Sampling is needed because researching a whole population is rarely practical: populations are large, contacting all of them costs more money and time than the decision can justify, and in many markets no complete list of the population exists to work from.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A sample result differs from the population figure by sampling error, which tends to fall as the sample grows but not in proportion to it. As an approximate guide for a percentage result, the margin of error is about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size: at 400 respondents that is about 5 percentage points either way, and reaching about 2.5 points requires about 1 600 respondents - four times the fieldwork for half the margin.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A sample misleads when the people in it differ systematically from the population, and size alone does not correct that: where respondents were chosen at one place, at one time of day, or because they were willing to stop and answer, a larger sample reproduces the same bias more precisely. Selecting respondents at random from the whole population, or setting quotas that match proportions already known about the population, reduces that risk, and neither removes the distortion caused by the people who decline to answer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Reliability is the degree to which data can be depended on to describe what it claims to describe, so that a decision taken on it rests on the market rather than on an artefact of how the data was collected.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Reliability is judged from how a set of findings was produced rather than from how the figures look: who collected the data and whether they had an interest in the result, how the respondents were selected and how many there were, how the questions were worded, when the data was collected, and how many of the people approached actually answered.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where the people who did not answer differ from those who did, the findings describe the respondents rather than the population. A satisfaction survey returned by 60 of 500 customers describes those 60; if dissatisfied customers were the more likely to ignore it, the resulting satisfaction figure is too high by an amount the data itself cannot reveal.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Data collected some time ago can be an accurate record of its own period and still be a poor guide to the present, because what it measured may have moved since it was collected. The risk grows with the age of the data and with the speed at which the market changes, so the same three-year-old figures may be sound for a staple food and misleading for mobile data prices.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Quantitative data is information in numerical form - how many, how much, how often - and can be totalled, averaged and compared. Qualitative data is information about opinions, reasons and attitudes, expressed in words, and is analysed by grouping answers into recurring themes and counting how often each theme appears, not by doing arithmetic on the answers themselves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Quantitative analysis at this level means totals, percentages and shares, averages and change over time. The mean is the total of the values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value once the values are put in order, or the midpoint of the two middle values where there is an even number of them. The mode is the value that occurs most often.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The mean is pulled towards extreme values and the median is not, so where a few unusually large or small figures sit in a set of data the two averages give different answers. A business that quotes only the mean can end up describing a typical customer that few of its customers resemble, and price or stock for that customer instead of the real ones.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Quantitative and qualitative data answer different questions. Numbers show how many and how much, so they can be scaled to the market and carried into a forecast. Words show why, so they explain the number and point at what could be changed. A number on its own leaves the business guessing at the reason, and a reason on its own leaves it guessing at the size.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Reading a table or a graph starts with what is being measured, in what units, over what period and for whom - the title, the column headings or axis labels, the units and the source - and only then with the shape of the numbers, because a figure read without those four things can be compared with something it is not comparable to.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A share and an absolute figure can move in opposite directions, so a business reading only one of them can reach the wrong conclusion: a producer whose share of a market falls from 20% to 18% while the market grows from 400 000 to 500 000 units has sold more units than before, 90 000 against 80 000, and is losing ground to rivals while its own sales rise.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A graph can be accurate in every number and still give a misleading impression. A vertical axis that does not start at zero makes a small change look large, a scale that changes part-way along distorts the slope, and a short run of periods can conceal the direction of a longer one. Reading the axis and the period before the shape of the line is what guards against this.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Two series that move together in a table or on a graph show an association, not a cause: the influence may run the other way, or both may be following something else that is not shown. Deciding which requires evidence beyond the pattern itself, such as a period in which one moves and the other does not, or a controlled test.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
